primary_meaning: The tares (darnel, Lolium temulentum) symbolize the 'sons of the evil one' — false believers or counterfeit Christians sown by the devil among the genuine 'sons of the kingdom' (the wheat). They look nearly identical to true believers until maturity, coexist with them until the end of the age, and are then separated out and destroyed at the final judgment by the angels. This meaning is unusually settled because Jesus himself supplies the interpretation within the Gospel text.
primary_basis: Matthew 13:24-30 (the Parable of the Wheat and the Tares)
Matthew 13:36-43 (Jesus' explicit interpretation: the good seed are the sons of the kingdom; the tares are the sons of the evil one; the enemy is the devil; the harvest is the end of the age)
Matthew 3:12 / Luke 3:17 (John the Baptist's wheat-and-chaff separation imagery, often cited as parallel)
Matthew 13:47-50 (Parable of the Dragnet, treated as a companion parable teaching the same end-time separation)

alternatives.meaning: Ecclesiological reading (corpus permixtum): the field is specifically the church, so the tares represent hypocrites and false members mixed within the visible church who must be tolerated (not forcibly rooted out) until God's judgment. Classic in Augustine's anti-Donatist polemic and much subsequent Catholic and magisterial Protestant teaching against premature purges, schism, or persecution.
basis: Matthew 13:24-30, especially v. 29-30 ('let both grow together until the harvest')
Augustine's anti-Donatist writings and later citation in debates over church discipline and religious coercion

alternatives.meaning: The field is the world, not the church: the parable teaches the coexistence of the righteous and the wicked in the world at large until final judgment, and is not primarily about church discipline. Advocated by many modern exegetes appealing to Matthew 13:38 ('the field is the world') against the Augustinian ecclesial reading.

Tares as false doctrine or heresy sown secretly by Satan (or by heretics) into Christ's teaching/community — an emphasis found in some patristic writers (e.g., strands in Irenaeus, Chrysostom's homilies treat the tares as heretics) and in later polemical use.
basis: Matthew 13:25 ('while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares')
Patristic homiletic tradition (e.g., Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew)

alternatives.meaning: Tolerationist political reading: the parable as a proof-text against capital punishment of heretics and against state religious coercion (used by Roger Williams, some Anabaptists, and Enlightenment-era toleration arguments) — an application built on the standard meaning rather than a different identification of the tares.
basis: Roger Williams, 'The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution' and similar toleration literature

alternatives.meaning: Gnostic or esoteric readings in which the tares represent an evil admixture in creation or in the soul sown by a lower power; some modern devotional readings similarly internalize the parable as good and evil impulses within each person.
basis: Gospel of Thomas 57 (parallel parable used in some historical-critical discussion)
Assorted gnostic and modern spiritualizing commentary

notes: This is one of the most settled symbols in Christian interpretation because the Gospel itself decodes it (Matt 13:36-43): tares = sons of the evil one / false counterfeits among the true. The genuine interpretive disputes concern secondary questions — whether the 'field' is the world or the church, and what pastoral or political conclusions follow about tolerating evil until judgment — not the core identification of the tares with the wicked or counterfeit believers. Botanical background (darnel's near-indistinguishability from wheat before heading) is routinely used to underline the counterfeit theme.
